summary: Simplified Multicast Forwarding (SMF) provides basic IP multicast forwarding for limited wireless mesh and mobile ad hoc networks, where efficient flooding is an acceptable design. It defines duplicate packet detection for IPv4 and IPv6 and optional reduced relay sets. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: Simplified Multicast Forwarding (SMF) helps multicast packets reach routers in a wireless mesh or mobile ad hoc network. It detects packets that have already been forwarded and can choose a smaller set of routers to repeat them.

subtitle: Best-effort multicast forwarding for wireless mesh and mobile ad hoc networks.

tldr.problem: Wireless mesh and mobile ad hoc networks may need a simple way to deliver multicast packets when maintaining a forwarding tree is impractical.
tldr.mechanism: Simplified Multicast Forwarding (SMF) floods multicast packets while detecting duplicates, and can use selected relay sets to reduce repeated transmissions.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines an Experimental, best-effort forwarding mechanism for IPv4 and IPv6 within a MANET routing domain.

today: RFC 6621 is Experimental. It defines best-effort SMF forwarding and duplicate detection for IPv4 and IPv6 in limited MANET settings.

sections.title: A Basic Multicast Service for MANETs
sections.content:
SMF provides best-effort multicast forwarding in a single mobile ad hoc network routing domain. The design is intended for settings where controlled flooding is an acceptable trade-off, rather than maintaining a conventional multicast forwarding tree.

The RFC defines duplicate detection for both IPv4 and IPv6 and describes optional reduced relay sets. SMF can use neighbor information from another running protocol or from a neighborhood-discovery process.
sections.plainLanguage: SMF spreads multicast packets through a wireless ad hoc network. It is meant for limited network areas where flooding is useful and does not have to guarantee delivery.

sections.title: Flooding and Packet Forwarding
sections.content:
With Classic Flooding, each SMF router forwards each unique multicast packet once. This simple mode needs no relay-set selection, but it can send unnecessary copies and increase network contention.

Before forwarding, an SMF router checks that the packet is multicast, has a hop limit above one, is not link-local, and has not already been forwarded. The router decreases the hop limit before sending the packet onward.
sections.plainLanguage: In basic flooding, routers repeat a multicast packet once and ignore copies they have already seen. The hop limit and packet type determine whether a router may forward it.

sections.title: Detecting Duplicate Packets
sections.content:
Wireless routers can hear the same packet from several neighbors or on more than one interface. SMF keeps a history of recently processed packets to avoid forwarding duplicates across the network.

The RFC describes identification-based detection, which uses packet identifiers or header information, and hash-based detection, which compares a hash of packet contents. Routers in one SMF deployment must use compatible detection approaches.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers remember recently handled packets so they do not keep repeating the same message. They can compare packet identifiers or compare a hash made from packet contents.

sections.title: Reduced Relay Sets and Boundaries
sections.content:
A reduced relay set selects only some routers to forward multicast packets. This can lower the number of repeated transmissions, but selecting and maintaining the relays generally requires information about nearby routers.

The RFC also discusses how SMF can interact with multicast routing outside the MANET through a border router or proxy. It identifies border-router behavior as an area where further work remains.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of asking every router to repeat a packet, SMF can choose a connected subset of relays. A border router is needed when the MANET exchanges multicast traffic with other multicast networks.
